    1. Two equations that were stopped early . Foundational, 10 points. Question 1 of 5.

    Foundational 10 pts

    Both equations below have real coefficients and a negative discriminant, and there is nothing wrong with either of them. What was missing when you first met this situation was not a method but a supply of numbers wide enough for the method to land in. Nothing about the quadratic formula changes here. What changes is that you do not stop.

    Hints

    One at a time, each one a step further than the last. Take only as many as you need.

    1. Hint 1 of 3

      Nothing about the method changes when the discriminant turns out negative. The only new move is reading the square root of a negative number as iii times a real square root, at the moment it appears, and then insisting that the denominator gets applied to the whole numerator.

    2. Hint 2 of 3 · Part B

      You now have two radicands to compare, 363636 and 282828. Ask what has to be true of a positive integer before its square root can be written as a fraction of integers, and check both of yours against that.

    3. Hint 3 of 3 · Part C

      Split the formula into the piece that contains the radical and the piece that does not, and ask separately of each one whether it is a real number and whether the sign in front of it varies between the two roots.

    That is every hint for this question.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    With a=2a = 2a=2, b=−10b = -10b=−10 and c=17c = 17c=17, compute the discriminant first, because its sign decides what kind of answer you are heading for.

    Δ=(−10)2−4(2)(17)=100−136=−36\Delta = (-10)^2 - 4(2)(17) = 100 - 136 = -36Δ=(−10)2−4(2)(17)=100−136=−36

    It is negative, so no real number solves this equation and the formula is about to ask for the square root of a negative number. Read that root in iii-form the moment it appears, −36=6i\sqrt{-36} = 6i−36​=6i, and then carry on exactly as usual with 2a=42a = 42a=4:

    x=−(−10)±−362(2)=10±6i4x = \frac{-(-10) \pm \sqrt{-36}}{2(2)} = \frac{10 \pm 6i}{4}x=2(2)−(−10)±−36​​=410±6i​

Two cheap checks are available and worth the seconds. The roots should add to −ba=5-\frac{b}{a} = 5−ab​=5, and they do, because the imaginary parts cancel. Their product should be ca=172\frac{c}{a} = \frac{17}{2}ac​=217​, and it is:

    (52)2+(32)2=254+94=344=172\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{25}{4} + \frac{9}{4} = \frac{34}{4} = \frac{17}{2}(25​)2+(23​)2=425​+49​=434​=217​

    Part B

    Take the discriminant first again, with a=1a = 1a=1, b=2b = 2b=2 and c=8c = 8c=8:

    Δ=22−4(1)(8)=4−32=−28\Delta = 2^2 - 4(1)(8) = 4 - 32 = -28Δ=22−4(1)(8)=4−32=−28

    Now −28=i28=i4⋅7=2i7\sqrt{-28} = i\sqrt{28} = i\sqrt{4 \cdot 7} = 2i\sqrt{7}−28​=i28​=i4⋅7​=2i7​, and with 2a=22a = 22a=2 both terms of the numerator are halved:

    x=−2±2i72=−1±i7x = \frac{-2 \pm 2i\sqrt{7}}{2} = -1 \pm i\sqrt{7}x=2−2±2i7​​=−1±i7​

    The sum is −2=−ba-2 = -\frac{b}{a}−2=−ab​ and the product is 1+7=8=ca1 + 7 = 8 = \frac{c}{a}1+7=8=ac​, so both roots check out.

    Now the comparison. In both equations the imaginary part is

    q=∣Δ∣2a,q = \frac{\sqrt{|\Delta|}}{2a},q=2a∣Δ∣​​,

    and 2a2a2a is an integer, so everything turns on whether ∣Δ∣\sqrt{|\Delta|}∣Δ∣​ is rational. Here ∣Δ∣|\Delta|∣Δ∣ is a positive integer, and the square root of a positive integer is either an integer or irrational, never a fraction in between. So, for an equation of this kind with Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0, qqq is rational exactly when ∣Δ∣|\Delta|∣Δ∣ is a perfect square. Both directions of that hold: if ∣Δ∣=m2|\Delta| = m^2∣Δ∣=m2 then ∣Δ∣=m\sqrt{|\Delta|} = m∣Δ∣​=m and qqq is rational, and if qqq is rational then ∣Δ∣=2aq\sqrt{|\Delta|} = 2aq∣Δ∣​=2aq is rational and therefore an integer, which makes ∣Δ∣|\Delta|∣Δ∣ a perfect square.

    That is exactly what separated the two equations:

    ∣−36∣=62,∣−28∣≠m2 for any integer m|-36| = 6^2, \qquad |-28| \ne m^2 \text{ for any integer } m∣−36∣=62,∣−28∣=m2 for any integer m

    Keep the negative discriminant attached to that statement, because it is what puts the radical in the imaginary part in the first place. When Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0 the same radical lands in the real part instead, and the roots of x2−3x^2 - 3x2−3 have imaginary part 000 though 121212 is no perfect square. The mechanism is not new: the imaginary part inherits whatever the radical leaves behind, exactly as an irrational real root did when the discriminant was positive.

    Part C

    The formula produces the two roots from one expression, and the only difference between them is the sign in front of the second piece. So whatever the first piece is, both roots contain it unchanged, and whatever the second piece is, one root adds it and the other subtracts it.

    The first piece is −b2a-\frac{b}{2a}−2ab​. It is built from the coefficients alone, with no radical in it, so it is a real number for every real a≠0a \ne 0a=0 and bbb, no matter what the discriminant does. It is the axis of symmetry, exactly as it was when the roots were real.

    The second piece is where the sign of Δ\DeltaΔ lands. When Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0, write Δ=i∣Δ∣\sqrt{\Delta} = i\sqrt{|\Delta|}Δ​=i∣Δ∣​, and the offset becomes

    Δ2a=∣Δ∣2a i,\frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a} = \frac{\sqrt{|\Delta|}}{2a}\,i,2aΔ​​=2a∣Δ∣​​i,

    which is a real number times iii. Naming the two pieces p=−b2ap = -\frac{b}{2a}p=−2ab​ and q=∣Δ∣2aq = \frac{\sqrt{|\Delta|}}{2a}q=2a∣Δ∣​​, both of them real, the formula reads

    x=p+qiandx=p−qi.x = p + qi \quad\text{and}\quad x = p - qi.x=p+qiandx=p−qi.

    The shared real part is forced by the shape of the formula, and the opposite imaginary parts are forced by the ±\pm±. So the answer to the second question is that the centre does not change character at all: it is real before and after. The offset does. When Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0 it is a real distance and the ±\pm± moves the two roots left and right along the number line; when Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0 the same ±\pm± moves them the same distance up and down instead, off the line and on opposite sides of it. The roots still straddle the axis. They have simply stopped straddling it along the line.

    In one line

    The first equation gives 52±32i\frac{5}{2} \pm \frac{3}{2}i25​±23​i and the second gives −1±i7-1 \pm i\sqrt{7}−1±i7​. With integer coefficients and a negative discriminant, the imaginary part is rational exactly when ∣Δ∣|\Delta|∣Δ∣ is a perfect square, which 363636 is and 282828 is not. In both equations the centre −b2a-\frac{b}{2a}−2ab​ is real and unchanged by the sign of Δ\DeltaΔ; only the offset changes character, from a real displacement along the line to an imaginary one across it.

    Another way: Complete the square instead of quoting the formula

    The first equation can be finished without the formula at all. Take the 222 out of the first two terms and complete the square inside:

    2x2−10x+17=2(x−52)2−252+17=2(x−52)2+922x^2 - 10x + 17 = 2\left(x - \frac{5}{2}\right)^2 - \frac{25}{2} + 17 = 2\left(x - \frac{5}{2}\right)^2 + \frac{9}{2}2x2−10x+17=2(x−25​)2−225​+17=2(x−25​)2+29​

    Setting that to 000 gives (x−52)2=−94\left(x - \frac{5}{2}\right)^2 = -\frac{9}{4}(x−25​)2=−49​, and a negative number has exactly two square roots, both pure imaginary:

    x−52=±32ix - \frac{5}{2} = \pm\frac{3}{2}ix−25​=±23​i

    which is the same pair. This is worth doing once, because it shows where the centre and the offset in part C come from: the completed square puts the centre on the left and the offset on the right before any root is taken.

    When it is worth it When you want to see the centre and the offset as separate objects, or when the leading coefficient is small enough that completing the square is quicker than substituting into the formula.

    2. Taking the hypothesis away . Reasoning, 16 points. Question 2 of 5.

    Reasoning 16 pts

    The formula returns a conjugate pair every time, which leaves an obvious question open: is that a habit of the formula, or a law about the equations? It is a law, and like every law it carries a hypothesis. This question proves the law, then withdraws the hypothesis to find out what it was holding up.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Let aaa, bbb and ccc be real with a≠0a \ne 0a=0, and suppose the complex number zzz satisfies az2+bz+c=0az^2 + bz + c = 0az2+bz+c=0. Prove that z‾\overline{z}z satisfies it too. Beside each step, name which of these three facts you used: that conjugation respects sums, that it respects products, or that a real number is its own conjugate. Then say at which single line your proof first uses the reality of aaa, bbb and ccc, and how much of the argument still stands without that assumption.

      Complete the derivation Each line should follow from the one above it. Say what lets you take each step. 6 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Now withdraw the hypothesis. Build a quadratic with at least one non-real coefficient whose two roots are one real number and one non-real number. Verify that both of your numbers are roots, show that the conjugate of the non-real one is not, and say why none of this contradicts part A.

      Construct a counterexample Give one specific case, and show it breaks the claim. 5 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Part A settles one direction of a possible equivalence: real coefficients force the non-real roots into conjugate pairs. Test the other direction. If a quadratic's non-real roots come in conjugate pairs, must its coefficients be real? Report the status of the equivalence as a whole, and if either direction fails, state an extra condition that repairs it.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 5 points

    Hints

    One at a time, each one a step further than the last. Take only as many as you need.

    1. Hint 1 of 4

      The proof of this theorem uses three separate facts about conjugation, and only one of them says anything at all about the coefficients. Find that one first, because everything in this question is organised around what happens when it is unavailable.

    2. Hint 2 of 4 · Part B

      A quadratic is far easier to build from the roots you want than to find by hunting for coefficients. Decide on a root inventory the theorem rules out, then multiply the two linear factors together and read off what the coefficients turned out to be.

    3. Hint 3 of 4 · Part C

      One direction of the claim is already proved and needs no further work. For the other one, ask whether you can keep a pair of roots exactly where they are while spoiling the coefficients.

    4. Hint 4 of 4 · Part C

      Multiplying an equation through by a nonzero constant never moves a root, and nothing says that constant has to be a real number.

    That is every hint for this question.

    Answer and solution

    Check your answer first. If it is wrong, go back to your paper: the worked solution will still be here.

    The answer

    Part A

    Conjugating the whole equation gives az‾ 2+bz‾+c=0a\overline{z}^{\,2} + b\overline{z} + c = 0az2+bz+c=0, so z‾\overline{z}z is a root. Splitting the sum and the products needs no hypothesis at all; the reality of the coefficients is used exactly once, to turn a‾\overline{a}a, b‾\overline{b}b and c‾\overline{c}c back into aaa, bbb and ccc.

    Part B

    One example is x2−(2+3i)x+6i=0x^2 - (2 + 3i)x + 6i = 0x2−(2+3i)x+6i=0, built as (x−2)(x−3i)(x - 2)(x - 3i)(x−2)(x−3i). Its roots are 222 and 3i3i3i, while substituting −3i-3i−3i gives −18+12i-18 + 12i−18+12i, which is not 000. Part A never applied, because the coefficients −(2+3i)-(2 + 3i)−(2+3i) and 6i6i6i are not real.

    • Any product (x−r)(x−s)(x - r)(x - s)(x−r)(x−s) with rrr real and sss non-real works. Multiplying it out puts −(r+s)-(r + s)−(r+s) and rsrsrs in the coefficient slots, and the middle one is never real, which is all the question asks for; the constant rsrsrs is non-real as well whenever r≠0r \ne 0r=0

    Part C

    The biconditional is false. Its forward direction is exactly part A, but the converse fails: ix2−6ix+34iix^2 - 6ix + 34iix2−6ix+34i has the conjugate pair 3±5i3 \pm 5i3±5i as its roots and not one real coefficient. Requiring the leading coefficient to be real repairs the converse.

    Not what you got? Look for the slip on your own paper before you open the solution. Finding it yourself is worth more than reading it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Conjugation is a function, so it may be applied to both sides of a true equation and the two sides stay equal. Apply it to az2+bz+c=0az^2 + bz + c = 0az2+bz+c=0 and work on each side.

    The right side is 000, a real number, so it is its own conjugate. That is the third fact, used here on the right side and due to return at the end for the coefficients:

    0‾=0\overline{0} = 00=0

    The left side is a sum of three terms, and conjugation respects sums, so it passes through both plus signs. That is the first fact:

    az2+bz+c‾=az2‾+bz‾+c‾\overline{az^2 + bz + c} = \overline{az^2} + \overline{bz} + \overline{c}az2+bz+c​=az2+bz+c

    Each of the first two terms is a product, and conjugation respects products, so it passes through those as well. That is the second fact, and it is applied three times here: once to separate aaa from z2z^2z2, once to separate bbb from zzz, and once more on z2=z⋅zz^2 = z \cdot zz2=z⋅z, which gives z2‾=z‾ z‾=z‾ 2\overline{z^2} = \overline{z}\,\overline{z} = \overline{z}^{\,2}z2=zz=z2:

    az2‾+bz‾+c‾=a‾ z‾ 2+b‾ z‾+c‾\overline{az^2} + \overline{bz} + \overline{c} = \overline{a}\,\overline{z}^{\,2} + \overline{b}\,\overline{z} + \overline{c}az2+bz+c=az2+bz+c

    Stop and look at that line, because it is true for every quadratic whatsoever, with any complex coefficients at all. No hypothesis has been spent yet.

    The hypothesis is spent on the very next line, and only there. Since aaa, bbb and ccc are real, each is its own conjugate, so a‾=a\overline{a} = aa=a, b‾=b\overline{b} = bb=b and c‾=c\overline{c} = cc=c, and the three barred coefficients turn back into the original three:

    0=az‾ 2+bz‾+c0 = a\overline{z}^{\,2} + b\overline{z} + c0=az2+bz+c

    That expression is the original quadratic evaluated at z‾\overline{z}z, and it equals 000, so z‾\overline{z}z is a root. Notice what the theorem does and does not say. If zzz happens to be real then z‾=z\overline{z} = zz=z and the conclusion is no news. Its whole force is on non-real roots, which it forbids from ever turning up alone.

    Part B

    Hunting for coefficients would be slow. Build the quadratic from the roots you want instead, since a quadratic with roots rrr and sss and leading coefficient 111 is (x−r)(x−s)(x - r)(x - s)(x−r)(x−s). The root inventory to aim for is the one the theorem forbids for real coefficients: one real root and one non-real root. Take r=2r = 2r=2 and s=3is = 3is=3i and multiply out:

    (x−2)(x−3i)=x2−3ix−2x+6i=x2−(2+3i)x+6i(x - 2)(x - 3i) = x^2 - 3ix - 2x + 6i = x^2 - (2 + 3i)x + 6i(x−2)(x−3i)=x2−3ix−2x+6i=x2−(2+3i)x+6i

    Both of the chosen numbers are roots, which the factored form already guarantees, but substitute to be sure. At x=2x = 2x=2:

    4−(2+3i)(2)+6i=4−4−6i+6i=04 - (2 + 3i)(2) + 6i = 4 - 4 - 6i + 6i = 04−(2+3i)(2)+6i=4−4−6i+6i=0

    At x=3ix = 3ix=3i, using (3i)2=−9(3i)^2 = -9(3i)2=−9 and (2+3i)(3i)=6i+9i2=−9+6i(2 + 3i)(3i) = 6i + 9i^2 = -9 + 6i(2+3i)(3i)=6i+9i2=−9+6i:

    −9−(−9+6i)+6i=−9+9−6i+6i=0-9 - (-9 + 6i) + 6i = -9 + 9 - 6i + 6i = 0−9−(−9+6i)+6i=−9+9−6i+6i=0

    Now test the conjugate of the non-real root. At x=−3ix = -3ix=−3i, using (−3i)2=−9(-3i)^2 = -9(−3i)2=−9 and (2+3i)(−3i)=−6i−9i2=9−6i(2 + 3i)(-3i) = -6i - 9i^2 = 9 - 6i(2+3i)(−3i)=−6i−9i2=9−6i:

    −9−(9−6i)+6i=−18+12i-9 - (9 - 6i) + 6i = -18 + 12i−9−(9−6i)+6i=−18+12i

    That is not 000, so −3i-3i−3i is not a root. The quadratic has exactly two roots, one real and one not, and the non-real one stands alone.

    There is no contradiction with part A, because part A was never available here. Its hypothesis is that aaa, bbb and ccc are real, and this quadratic has b=−(2+3i)b = -(2 + 3i)b=−(2+3i) and c=6ic = 6ic=6i. The proof used that hypothesis at exactly one line, replacing b‾\overline{b}b by bbb and c‾\overline{c}c by ccc. Withdraw it and that line fails, and with it the conclusion. This is why the theorem is worth stating with its hypothesis attached every time: what fails without it is not a technicality but the whole result.

    Part C

    An if and only if is two claims, and they have to be tested one at a time.

    The forward direction, that real coefficients force the non-real roots into conjugate pairs, is precisely what part A proves. Nothing more is needed for it.

    The converse says that conjugate pairing forces the coefficients to be real, and it is false. The reason is that multiplying an equation through by any nonzero constant leaves its roots exactly where they were, and that constant does not have to be real. Start from a quadratic whose roots really are a conjugate pair:

    x2−6x+34=0hasx=6±36−1362=6±10i2=3±5ix^2 - 6x + 34 = 0 \quad\text{has}\quad x = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 136}}{2} = \frac{6 \pm 10i}{2} = 3 \pm 5ix2−6x+34=0hasx=26±36−136​​=26±10i​=3±5i

    Now multiply through by iii:

    ix2−6ix+34i=0ix^2 - 6ix + 34i = 0ix2−6ix+34i=0

Do not assume such a quadratic factors and then read bbb and ccc off the factorization; build it instead, since the hypothesis permits only two root inventories and each can be multiplied out directly.

    If both roots are real, say r1r_1r1​ and r2r_2r2​, then

    is real throughout as well.

    One case deserves naming, because it looks like a third inventory that would sink the repair: a repeated non-real root, as in x2−2ix−1=(x−i)2x^2 - 2ix - 1 = (x - i)^2x2−2ix−1=(x−i)2, whose leading coefficient 111 is perfectly real. It is not a counterexample, because the hypothesis rules it out rather than covering it. The root iii is non-real and its conjugate −i-i−i is not a root, since (−i−i)2=−4≠0(-i - i)^2 = -4 \ne 0(−i−i)2=−4=0, so this quadratic's non-real roots do not come in conjugate pairs. The two counterexamples earlier are excluded from the other side, by their leading coefficient of iii.

    In one line

Withdraw it and the result goes: x2−(2+3i)x+6ix^2 - (2 + 3i)x + 6ix2−(2+3i)x+6i has roots 222 and 3i3i3i, an inventory no real quadratic can have, and −3i-3i−3i is not a root. The equivalence is false as a biconditional. Its forward direction is the theorem, while its converse fails on ix2−6ix+34iix^2 - 6ix + 34iix2−6ix+34i, whose roots are the conjugate pair 3±5i3 \pm 5i3±5i and whose coefficients are all non-real; requiring a real leading coefficient repairs it.

    3. How much one root is worth . Application, 12 points. Question 3 of 5.

    Application 12 pts

    A quadratic carries three coefficients, so a single root looks like far too little information to pin one down. Each part below hands you one root, or one fact about a root, and asks what the coefficients are then obliged to be.

      Part A.

    They are not determined. The theorem hands back the root you already had, since 2‾=2\overline{2} = 22=2, so the second root is unconstrained: 3(x−2)(x−r)3(x - 2)(x - r)3(x−2)(x−r) has real coefficients and 222 as a root for every real rrr, giving 3x2−21x+303x^2 - 21x + 303x2−21x+30 at r=5r = 5r=5 and 3x2+9x−303x^2 + 9x - 303x2+9x−30 at r=−5r = -5r=−5.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The coefficients are real and one root is not, so the conjugate root theorem applies and hands over the second root at no cost: it is 1−4i1 - 4i1−4i. With both roots in hand the two totals finish the job.

    The sum of the roots is

    (1+4i)+(1−4i)=2,(1 + 4i) + (1 - 4i) = 2,(1+4i)+(1−4i)=2,

    and the sum equals −ba-\frac{b}{a}−ab​, so −b3=2-\frac{b}{3} = 2−3b​=2 and b=−6b = -6b=−6.

    The product is a conjugate product, so the iii terms cancel and what survives is the squared modulus of either root:

    (1+4i)(1−4i)=12+42=17(1 + 4i)(1 - 4i) = 1^2 + 4^2 = 17(1+4i)(1−4i)=12+42=17

    The product equals ca\frac{c}{a}ac​, so c3=17\frac{c}{3} = 173c​=17 and c=51c = 51c=51. The quadratic is 3x2−6x+513x^2 - 6x + 513x2−6x+51.

    Verify by solving it. The discriminant is (−6)2−4(3)(51)=36−612=−576(-6)^2 - 4(3)(51) = 36 - 612 = -576(−6)2−4(3)(51)=36−612=−576, and −576=24i\sqrt{-576} = 24i−576​=24i, so

    x=6±24i6=1±4i,x = \frac{6 \pm 24i}{6} = 1 \pm 4i,x=66±24i​=1±4i,

    returning the given root and its conjugate. One non-real root and a leading coefficient determined all three coefficients.

    Part B

    Run the same machinery and watch it stall. The theorem says that if zzz is a root then so is z‾\overline{z}z. Here z=2z = 2z=2 is real, and a real number is its own conjugate:

    2‾=2\overline{2} = 22=2

    So the theorem is perfectly true and completely uninformative. It returns the root already in hand and supplies no second root at all. Without a second root there is no sum and no product, so nothing determines bbb and ccc.

    That is not a gap in the argument; it is a fact about the quadratics themselves. Every quadratic 3(x−2)(x−r)3(x - 2)(x - r)3(x−2)(x−r) with rrr real has real coefficients and has 222 as a root, and different choices of rrr give genuinely different quadratics:

    3(x−2)(x−5)=3x2−21x+30,3(x−2)(x+5)=3x2+9x−303(x - 2)(x - 5) = 3x^2 - 21x + 30, \qquad 3(x - 2)(x + 5) = 3x^2 + 9x - 303(x−2)(x−5)=3x2−21x+30,3(x−2)(x+5)=3x2+9x−30

    Both have 222 as a root, both have real coefficients and leading coefficient 333, and they are not the same polynomial, so the data cannot possibly determine one answer. Infinitely many more come from other choices of rrr.

    The contrast with part A is the whole point, and it is not a contrast in difficulty. There the theorem manufactured a second root, and two roots plus a leading coefficient fix everything. Here it manufactures nothing, and one root plus a leading coefficient leaves a whole family standing. The theorem's force was never in the pairing rule as such; it is in what the pairing rule gives you when the root you are handed is not its own conjugate.

    Part C

    Write the root as z=p+qiz = p + qiz=p+qi with ppp and qqq real and q≠0q \ne 0q=0, since zzz is not real. The coefficients are real, so the other root is z‾=p−qi\overline{z} = p - qiz=p−qi, and being monic the quadratic is x2−(sum)x+(product)x^2 - (\text{sum})x + (\text{product})x2−(sum)x+(product).

    The product of the pair is the squared modulus, and the modulus is exactly the datum you were given:

    c=zz‾=p2+q2=∣z∣2=72=49c = z\overline{z} = p^2 + q^2 = |z|^2 = 7^2 = 49c=zz=p2+q2=∣z∣2=72=49

    So the constant term is pinned down completely, without knowing either part of the root separately. The distance from the origin is precisely the quantity the product measures.

    The sum is a different quantity, and the datum does not determine it, though it does not leave it entirely free either. The sum is 2p2p2p, so

    b=−2p,b = -2p,b=−2p,

    and ppp is not determined by ∣z∣=7|z| = 7∣z∣=7. All that is forced is p2+q2=49p^2 + q^2 = 49p2+q2=49 with q≠0q \ne 0q=0, which gives p2<49p^2 < 49p2<49, so ppp may be anywhere strictly between −7-7−7 and 777, and bbb anywhere strictly between −14-14−14 and 141414. Two members of the family show the spread:

    x2+49with roots ±7i,x2−10x+49with roots 5±2i6x^2 + 49 \quad\text{with roots } \pm 7i, \qquad x^2 - 10x + 49 \quad\text{with roots } 5 \pm 2i\sqrt{6}x2+49with roots ±7i,x2−10x+49with roots 5±2i6​

    Both are monic with real coefficients, and in both cases the root sits at distance 777 from the origin, since 02+72=490^2 + 7^2 = 4902+72=49 and 52+(26)2=25+24=495^2 + \left(2\sqrt{6}\right)^2 = 25 + 24 = 4952+(26​)2=25+24=49.

    The difference between the two coefficients is therefore a difference between the two totals. The product depends only on how far the root is from the origin, which you were told; the sum depends on where it sits along that circle of possibilities, which you were not, and all the datum can do for the sum is confine it to a range.

    In one line

    The first quadratic is 3x2−6x+513x^2 - 6x + 513x2−6x+51. A real nonzero root such as 222 determines neither bbb nor ccc, because the theorem returns that same root and leaves the second one free: 3(x−2)(x−r)3(x - 2)(x - r)3(x−2)(x−r) qualifies for every real rrr. For a monic quadratic with real coefficients and a non-real root of modulus 777, the constant term is fixed at 494949, since the product of the pair is the squared modulus, while b=−2pb = -2pb=−2p is left anywhere strictly between −14-14−14 and 141414.

    Another way: Multiply the two factors out instead of using the totals

    Once the conjugate root theorem has given you both roots, you can build the quadratic directly from its factors and skip the sum and product entirely:

    (x−(1+4i))(x−(1−4i))=((x−1)−4i)((x−1)+4i)\bigl(x - (1 + 4i)\bigr)\bigl(x - (1 - 4i)\bigr) = \bigl((x - 1) - 4i\bigr)\bigl((x - 1) + 4i\bigr)(x−(1+4i))(x−(1−4i))=((x−1)−4i)((x−1)+4i)

    Grouping the two factors like that turns the expansion into a difference of squares, and (4i)2=−16(4i)^2 = -16(4i)2=−16 flips the sign:

    (x−1)2−(4i)2=x2−2x+1+16=x2−2x+17(x - 1)^2 - (4i)^2 = x^2 - 2x + 1 + 16 = x^2 - 2x + 17(x−1)2−(4i)2=x2−2x+1+16=x2−2x+17

    Multiplying by the leading coefficient 333 gives 3x2−6x+513x^2 - 6x + 513x2−6x+51 again.

    When it is worth it When the root has an awkward imaginary part and you would rather group and square once than compute a sum and a product separately. It is also the version that makes the factorization visible, which matters when the question asks for factors rather than coefficients.

    (p+qi)(p−qi)=p2−q2i2=p2+q2=∣p+qi∣2(p + qi)(p - qi) = p^2 - q^2i^2 = p^2 + q^2 = |p + qi|^2(p+qi)(p−qi)=p2−q2i2=p2+q2=∣p+qi∣2

So each root sits at squared distance 18\frac{1}{8}81​ from the origin, and no solving was needed to say so. Notice also that the product came out positive, which it had to: p2+q2p^2 + q^2p2+q2 is a sum of squares with q≠0q \ne 0q=0.

    The discriminant is already known to be −16-16−16, so −16=4i\sqrt{-16} = 4i−16​=4i and, dividing the whole numerator by 2a=162a = 162a=16:

    8x2+4x+1=8(x+14−14i)(x+14+14i)8x^2 + 4x + 1 = 8\left(x + \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4}i\right)\left(x + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4}i\right)8x2+4x+1=8(x+41​−41​i)(x+41​+41​i)

Over the real numbers this quadratic was irreducible, since it has no real root and therefore no real linear factor. Over the complex numbers it splits, like every quadratic.

    Part C

    Start with the half that is right, because it is genuinely proved. If a real quadratic has non-real roots then they are a conjugate pair p±qip \pm qip±qi with q≠0q \ne 0q=0, so

    ca=p2+q2>0,\frac{c}{a} = p^2 + q^2 > 0,ac​=p2+q2>0,

    and aaa and ccc must share a sign. That is a true implication, and it is what part A observed.

    The classmate then read it in the other direction, and an implication does not travel backwards for free. A positive product says only that the two roots are not of opposite signs, and two real roots of the same sign multiply to a positive number just as happily as a conjugate pair does. The stated example settles it, and it is worth noticing that it has the same aaa and the same ccc as part A, so it satisfies the classmate's condition exactly:

    8x2−6x+1:Δ=(−6)2−4(8)(1)=36−32=4>08x^2 - 6x + 1: \quad \Delta = (-6)^2 - 4(8)(1) = 36 - 32 = 4 > 08x2−6x+1:Δ=(−6)2−4(8)(1)=36−32=4>0

    both real, both positive, and multiplying to 18\frac{1}{8}81​, the same product as before. So the condition on the signs of aaa and ccc cannot possibly decide the question: two quadratics that agree on aaa and ccc can disagree about where their roots live, because bbb is free to change and the discriminant depends on it.

    The accurate statement of what survives is the contrapositive. If ca≤0\frac{c}{a} \le 0ac​≤0 then the roots are certainly real, since Δ=b2−4ac≥b2≥0\Delta = b^2 - 4ac \ge b^2 \ge 0Δ=b2−4ac≥b2≥0 in that case. So the sign of ca\frac{c}{a}ac​ can rule non-real roots out but can never rule them in. Only the discriminant does that.

    In one line

    Δ=−16<0\Delta = -16 < 0Δ=−16<0, so the roots are non-real, with sum −12-\frac{1}{2}−21​ and product 18\frac{1}{8}81​, which is also the squared distance from the origin to each root. Solving gives −14±14i-\frac{1}{4} \pm \frac{1}{4}i−41​±41​i and the factorization 8(x+1−i4)(x+1+i4)8\left(x + \frac{1 - i}{4}\right)\left(x + \frac{1 + i}{4}\right)8(x+41−i​)(x+41+i​). The classmate's implication runs the wrong way: non-real roots force aaa and ccc to share a sign, but sharing a sign does not in turn force the roots off the real line, as 8x2−6x+18x^2 - 6x + 18x2−6x+1 shows with its real roots 12\frac{1}{2}21​ and 14\frac{1}{4}41​.

    5. Watching the two roots move . Reasoning, 12 points. Question 5 of 5.

    Reasoning 12 pts

    One equation, one letter, and a whole family at once: 2x2+8x+k=02x^2 + 8x + k = 02x2+8x+k=0 has real coefficients for every real kkk, and its roots move as kkk moves. Following them is the quickest way to see what the sign of the discriminant reports now that the complex numbers are available.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Find every real kkk for which 2x2+8x+k=02x^2 + 8x + k = 02x2+8x+k=0 has non-real roots, and solve the equation for k=12k = 12k=12.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 3 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Call the threshold you found in part A the boundary value. Describe where the two roots sit below it, at it, and above it, and how they move as kkk increases through it. Name the feature of their position that never changes, whatever kkk is.

      Carry your own answer forward Work from the boundary value you reported in part A, whatever it was. The credit here is for describing how the roots move on either side of your own threshold, not for that threshold agreeing with anyone else's.

      Explain what it means Words, not just symbols. Say what the number is telling you about the situation. 4 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Over the complex numbers, how many roots does 2x2+8x+k=02x^2 + 8x + k = 02x2+8x+k=0 have for each real kkk? Make the boundary case, the one where the two roots arrive at the same place, carry the same count as the others and justify it as carefully as the rest, then state what the sign of the discriminant does still settle.

      Carry your own answer forward Use your own boundary value from part A and your own description of the three cases from part B. What is being credited is the counting argument, not whether your boundary agrees with anyone else's.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 5 points

    Hints

    One at a time, each one a step further than the last. Take only as many as you need.

    1. Hint 1 of 3

      You do not need to run the quadratic formula once per case. Complete the square a single time with kkk still a letter, and all three situations fall out of the same line as three sign possibilities on one side.

    2. Hint 2 of 3 · Part B

      Whatever kkk does, the two roots stay the same distance either side of one fixed number. Find that number first, then ask what the plus or minus is measuring in each of the three situations.

    3. Hint 3 of 3 · Part C

      A factorization counts more honestly than a graph does, because it does not care whether two things landed in the same place. Write the boundary quadratic as a product of linear factors and count the factors.

    That is every hint for this question.

    Answer and solution

    Check your answer first. If it is wrong, go back to your paper: the worked solution will still be here.

    The answer

    Part A

    The roots are non-real exactly when k>8k > 8k>8. At k=12k = 12k=12 they are −2+i2-2 + i\sqrt{2}−2+i2​ and −2−i2-2 - i\sqrt{2}−2−i2​.

    Part B

    They are always placed symmetrically about −2-2−2, which is their midpoint in every case and their common real part once they leave the line. Below the boundary they are two real points either side of −2-2−2, closing in as kkk rises; at it they meet at −2-2−2; above it they sit one above and one below −2-2−2, separating again as kkk rises.

    Part C

    Exactly two for every real kkk, counted with multiplicity. At k=8k = 8k=8 the quadratic is 2(x+2)22(x + 2)^22(x+2)2, so its two linear factors are equal and the single number −2-2−2 is a root twice over. The sign of Δ\DeltaΔ no longer settles how many roots there are; it settles only where they are.

    Not what you got? Look for the slip on your own paper before you open the solution. Finding it yourself is worth more than reading it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    With a=2a = 2a=2, b=8b = 8b=8 and c=kc = kc=k, the discriminant is a function of kkk:

    Δ=82−4(2)(k)=64−8k\Delta = 8^2 - 4(2)(k) = 64 - 8kΔ=82−4(2)(k)=64−8k

    The coefficients are real, so the roots are non-real exactly when Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0. Solve that inequality:

    64−8k<0⟺64<8k⟺k>864 - 8k < 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 64 < 8k \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad k > 864−8k<0⟺64<8k⟺k>8

    Both directions hold, since every step is reversible, so k>8k > 8k>8 is not merely sufficient but exactly the condition.

    At k=12k = 12k=12 the discriminant is 64−96=−3264 - 96 = -3264−96=−32, and −32=i16⋅2=4i2\sqrt{-32} = i\sqrt{16 \cdot 2} = 4i\sqrt{2}−32​=i16⋅2​=4i2​. Dividing the whole numerator by 2a=42a = 42a=4:

    x=−8±4i24=−2±i2x = \frac{-8 \pm 4i\sqrt{2}}{4} = -2 \pm i\sqrt{2}x=4−8±4i2​​=−2±i2​

    Check against the totals: the sum should be −ba=−4-\frac{b}{a} = -4−ab​=−4, and the two roots do add to −4-4−4; the product should be ca=6\frac{c}{a} = 6ac​=6, and (−2)2+(2)2=4+2=6(-2)^2 + \left(\sqrt{2}\right)^2 = 4 + 2 = 6(−2)2+(2​)2=4+2=6.

    Part B

    Completing the square once, with kkk left as a letter, gives every case at the same time:

    2x2+8x+k=2(x+2)2+(k−8)2x^2 + 8x + k = 2(x + 2)^2 + (k - 8)2x2+8x+k=2(x+2)2+(k−8)

    Setting that to 000 isolates the whole kkk dependence in one place:

    (x+2)2=8−k2(x + 2)^2 = \frac{8 - k}{2}(x+2)2=28−k​

    Now read the three cases off the right-hand side. If k<8k < 8k<8 it is positive, so x+2x + 2x+2 is a real number and

    x=−2±8−k2,x = -2 \pm \sqrt{\frac{8 - k}{2}},x=−2±28−k​​,

    two real points placed symmetrically either side of −2-2−2. At k=0k = 0k=0, for instance, they are −2±2-2 \pm 2−2±2, which is 000 and −4-4−4. As kkk rises toward 888 the square root shrinks and the two points close in on −2-2−2.

    If k=8k = 8k=8 the right-hand side is 000, so x+2=0x + 2 = 0x+2=0 and the two points have arrived at the same place, x=−2x = -2x=−2.

    If k>8k > 8k>8 the right-hand side is negative, and a negative number has two square roots, both pure imaginary:

    x=−2±k−82  ix = -2 \pm \sqrt{\frac{k - 8}{2}}\;ix=−2±2k−8​​i

    The two roots have left the line, one directly above −2-2−2 and one directly below, and as kkk rises further they move apart again in that new direction. At k=12k = 12k=12 this gives −2±i2-2 \pm i\sqrt{2}−2±i2​, agreeing with part A.

    What never changes is that −2-2−2 is the midpoint of the two roots. It is −b2a=−84-\frac{b}{2a} = -\frac{8}{4}−2ab​=−48​, a number built from aaa and bbb alone with no kkk in it, and the two roots sit symmetrically either side of it throughout: along the line while they are real, across it once they are not. Say midpoint rather than real part while the roots are still real, because there they are the numbers −2±(8−k)/2-2 \pm \sqrt{(8 - k)/2}−2±(8−k)/2​ and each is its own real part; at k=0k = 0k=0 the real parts are 000 and −4-4−4, not −2-2−2. Only once the roots leave the line does −2-2−2 become the real part they share.

    Part C

    Take the count first. For k≠8k \ne 8k=8 part B produced two roots whose offset from −2-2−2 is a nonzero number, real when k<8k < 8k<8 and imaginary when k>8k > 8k>8, so the two are distinct and there are plainly two of them.

    The case k=8k = 8k=8 is the one that looks like an exception, and a picture will not settle it, because the parabola touches the axis at a single point. A factorization settles it honestly. At k=8k = 8k=8,

    2x2+8x+8=2(x+2)2=2(x−(−2))(x−(−2))2x^2 + 8x + 8 = 2(x + 2)^2 = 2\bigl(x - (-2)\bigr)\bigl(x - (-2)\bigr)2x2+8x+8=2(x+2)2=2(x−(−2))(x−(−2))

    There are two linear factors, exactly as in every other case; they simply happen to be the same factor twice. So −2-2−2 is a root of multiplicity two, and the count is two again. Counting roots by how many different numbers you can see is what makes this case look smaller than the others; counting linear factors does not.

    So for every real kkk the equation has exactly two roots counted with multiplicity, and the count never moves. That is a genuine change from what the discriminant used to do. Over the real numbers its sign reported a count: two roots, one, or none. It cannot be reporting a count now, because the count is constant.

    What it still settles is where the two roots are:

    Δ>0: two distinct points of the real line,Δ=0: one point of the line, taken twice\Delta > 0: \text{ two distinct points of the real line}, \qquad \Delta = 0: \text{ one point of the line, taken twice}Δ>0: two distinct points of the real line,Δ=0: one point of the line, taken twice

    Δ<0: a conjugate pair off the line, one above it and one below\Delta < 0: \text{ a conjugate pair off the line, one above it and one below}Δ<0: a conjugate pair off the line, one above it and one below

    The negative discriminant that once ended the problem now only says that the two roots have stepped off the real line. It never meant that they were missing; it meant that they were somewhere the real numbers could not reach.

    In one line

    The roots are non-real exactly when k>8k > 8k>8, and at k=12k = 12k=12 they are −2±i2-2 \pm i\sqrt{2}−2±i2​. For every kkk they sit symmetrically about −2-2−2: apart along the real line while k<8k < 8k<8, together at −2-2−2 when k=8k = 8k=8, and one above and one below the line once k>8k > 8k>8. Over the complex numbers the count is two with multiplicity for every real kkk, so the sign of the discriminant no longer counts the roots. It locates them.

    Another way: One completed square answers all three parts

    Every question in this problem is answered by the single identity

    2x2+8x+k=2(x+2)2+(k−8),2x^2 + 8x + k = 2(x + 2)^2 + (k - 8),2x2+8x+k=2(x+2)2+(k−8),

    which you can obtain once and then never repeat. Setting it to zero gives (x+2)2=8−k2(x + 2)^2 = \frac{8 - k}{2}(x+2)2=28−k​, and from that one line: the roots are non-real exactly when the right side is negative, that is when k>8k > 8k>8; the centre is −2-2−2 for every kkk, since it is the number being squared; and the boundary k=8k = 8k=8 is the case where the right side is 000, which makes the quadratic 2(x+2)22(x + 2)^22(x+2)2 and the repeated root visible without any further work.

    The discriminant route reaches the same place, since 8−k2=64−8k16=Δ4a2\frac{8 - k}{2} = \frac{64 - 8k}{16} = \frac{\Delta}{4a^2}28−k​=1664−8k​=4a2Δ​.

    When it is worth it When a coefficient is a parameter. Completing the square keeps the parameter in one place, whereas the formula reintroduces it inside a radical every time you use it.

  • Constructs a quadratic from a deliberately chosen root inventory of one real and one non-real number, rather than guessing at coefficients. 3
  • Substitutes to confirm both chosen numbers are roots and that the conjugate of the non-real one is not, showing the arithmetic that produces a nonzero value. 1
  • Accounts for the absence of a contradiction by pointing at the hypothesis this quadratic fails, rather than by treating part A as having exceptions. 1

Part C 5

  • Treats the two directions separately, taking part A as settling one of them and testing the other on its own evidence, then reports the status of the equivalence as a whole. 3
  • Supplies a specific quadratic for the failing direction and shows its roots are what the claim assumes, then names a repairing condition and says why it closes the gap. 2

3. How much one root is worth 12 points

Part A 4

  • Obtains the second root from the first by conjugation, and says which hypothesis licenses that step. 2
  • Arrives at the correct bbb and ccc by any correct route, whether through the two totals or by expanding the two conjugate factors, with the stipulated leading coefficient 333 carried through rather than the monic quadratic reported in its place. 2

Part B 4

  • Rules that the coefficients are not determined, and grounds the ruling on the theorem returning the same root rather than on any failed calculation. 3
  • Exhibits at least two different quadratics meeting every stated condition, so that the claim of underdetermination is demonstrated and not merely asserted. 1

Part C 4

  • Connects the constant term to the product of the pair and the product to the squared modulus, so that the value of ccc follows from the given distance alone. 2
  • Explains that the sum is a separate quantity the given distance does not fix, and reports the range left open for bbb rather than declaring it simply unknown. 2

4. Two totals that never mentioned the real line 12 points

Part A 3

  • Computes the discriminant and classifies the roots as non-real from its sign, then reads the sum and the product off the coefficients as −ba-\frac{b}{a}−ab​ and ca\frac{c}{a}ac​ without first finding the roots. 2
  • Identifies the product of the conjugate pair with the squared modulus, and reports the squared distance for each root rather than for the pair jointly. 1

Part B 4

  • Divides the entire numerator by 2a2a2a, so both the real and the imaginary part of each root carry the division. 2
  • Writes the factorization as leading coefficient times two linear factors built from the roots, keeping the leading coefficient rather than dropping it, and confirms it by expanding. 2

Part C 5

  • Names the error as a reversed implication and states both directions separately, marking one as proved and the other as false. 3
  • Settles the classmate's example by computing its discriminant and its roots, showing they satisfy the sign condition while being real. 2

5. Watching the two roots move 12 points

Part A 3

  • Reduces the question to an inequality in kkk by any correct route, whether through the discriminant or through a completed square, and solves it rather than testing individual values of kkk. 2
  • Reports the condition on kkk as the exact range for which the roots are non-real, and gives both roots at k=12k = 12k=12 in the form p+qip + qip+qi. 1

Part B 4

  • Gives all three cases, including the boundary case, and describes the roots as moving continuously toward the boundary and away from it rather than as three unrelated situations. 3
  • Identifies the unchanging midpoint as −b2a-\frac{b}{2a}−2ab​, notes that it contains no kkk, and does not call it the roots' real part in the cases where the roots are real numbers other than it. 1

Part C 5

  • States the count as two with multiplicity for every real kkk, and argues the boundary case from a factorization into two linear factors rather than from the graph. 3
  • Contrasts what the sign of the discriminant used to report with what it reports now, and gives the three locations it distinguishes. 2
